abstract: Resilience is shaped by factors ranging from the genome through early-life experience to the brain, yet its biological basis in humans remains unclear because studies have rarely integrated these levels and have been confined to small samples. Using the Brief Resilience Scale (BRS) and multimodal data from tens of thousands of UK Biobank (UKB) participants, with replication in Generation Scotland (GS), we found that resting-state functional connectivity, particularly within the flexibility and valuation networks, is a robust neural correlate of resilience. Resilience also showed a generalizable genetic basis: a polygenic score (PGS) derived from a UKB genome-wide association study predicted BRS in GS. Genes and childhood experiences converged on the flexibility network through distinct routes: the polygenic association with resilience was partly explained by central executive-salience integration, whereas childhood experiences were associated with default-mode-centered integration. By separating genetically anchored from experience-sensitive routes, these findings point to network targets that interventions could tailor to the sources of an individual's vulnerability.
